background.definition: A keloid is an indolent, benign growth extending beyond margins of initial tissue damage, whereas hypertrophic scars are limited by the border of the original wound. Keloids may cause pain or functional impairment in certain anatomic regions, and recurrences are frequent.

list.listitem: Approximately 10% of the black, Hispanic and Asian population in the United States has a predisposition to keloid formation.
Darkly pigmented skin carries a 15-fold increase in risk, and there tends to be a familial predisposition.
Keloids are common in younger persons, peaking between 10 and 20 years of age.
Surgical incisions
Body piercing
Burn injury
Acne
Varicella lesions
Immunizations (especially Bacillus Calmette-Guérin)
Patients with keloid scarring have increased fibroblast proliferation rates.
Also, their collagen fibers are larger, thicker, and more wavy with random orientation.
Finally, there may be elevated enzyme concentrations and metabolic activity related to scar formation.

list.listitem: Keloid is an enlarging lesion in an area of previous tissue trauma. It typically extends beyond the margins of the original wound, and does not regress after 3 months.
They are typically raised and firm, with no drainage. Pain is common, but not always present.
Keloids are more frequent on earlobes, upper arms, cheeks, shoulders and the central anterior chest wall.
Biopsy is indicated if the lesion has bleeding, ulceration or irregular pigmentation. It is also indicated if the diagnosis cannot be established by history and physical.

Typical biopsy findings with keloid include collagen fibers that are larger, thicker, wavy, and have random orientation. Biopsy should be performed with minimal tssue trauma to prevent further growth of keloid.
Regression of keloid with steroid injection supports the diagnosis of keloid, although hypertrophic scar also will respond to steroid injection.
Identify patients at risk for keloid based on personal or family history.
Consider using intralesional corticosteroids or silicone gel sheeting to prevent keloid and hypertrophic scars.
If keloid occurs, treatment options include intralesional corticosteroids, 5-FU injections or "tattooing", and intralesional verapamil.

While guidelines recommend the use of intralesional corticosteroid injections and silicone gel or sheeting as first-line therapy for hypertrophic or keloid scars, C very low-certainty evidence supports their use. B
Second-line treatment options include intralesional 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), bleomycin, or verapamil, also based on very low-certainty evidence. B
Evidence is uncertain for the efficacy and safety of laser therapy in the treatment of hypertrophic and keloid scars. B
For recalcitrant keloid scars, consider surgical excision followed by radiation therapy to prevent recurrence. B

A systematic review identified 108 prospective studies of keloid therapies, including 37 randomized trials. They concluded that intralesional corticosteroid injections and silicone gel or sheeting as first-line therapies. Alternatives include intralesional 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), bleomycin, or verapamil with studies showing mixed results. Laser therapy may enhance drug penetration based on weak evidence. Finally, for persistent or recalcitrant lesions, excision followed by radiation therapy may be effective.

Intralesional steroids may be effective. Triamcinolone 10 or 40 mg/ml is usually used, and can be diluted with lidocaine to reduce discomfort. Two or three injections are usually performed at 4- to 6-week intervals. A small syringe (1 cc) and needle (25-30 gauge) should be used for injections. The solution is injected into the keloid until blanching of the keloid is seen. The typical dose is 10 mg per linear centimeter of keloid. The total dose of triamcinolone should not exceed 40 mg per session. Extralesional injections should be avoided as they may increase the risk of skin and tissue atrophy, telangiectasias and pigment changes. These occur in approximately 50% of patients. Systemic steroid effects are rare, but possible. Steroid injections should be discontinued if there is no response after the third treatment.
A meta-analysis concluded that there was limited evidence to support the combination of 5-FU and triamcinolone using a needle-free jet injector.
5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)

Postoperative serial intralesional injections or intraoperative topical administration of 5-FU have reduced the incidence of keloid formation in retropsective and prospective trials. 5-FU (50 mg/ml) is injected at 0.05 ml per linear centimeter every three weeks for up to 10 times. A pledget soaked in 5-FU (50 mg/ml) may alternately be placed for 5 minutes in the open wound prior to closure.

A systematic review of 40 studies with 2325 patients (not limited to RCTs) concluded that 5-FU is effective at reducing lesion size and reducing the likelihood of recurrence. Quality of evidence was limited though.

Intralesional verapamil: Intralesional injection of verapamil (2.5 mg/ml in a dose of 0.5-2.0 ml) given at 7, 14, 28, and 60 days was helpful in preventing keloid (90% vs 18% complete or partial success) in a study of 44 patients.

A meta-analysis for ear keloid treatment after surgical excision identified 25 studies with recurrence rates for ear keloid with triamcinolone treatment at 15.4% (95% CI, 9.4%-24.1%; p <0.001) and recurrence rate in the radiation group 14% (95% CI, 9.6%-19.9%; p <0.001). There was no significant difference between both treatments.
An RCT compared 5-FU tattooing with intralesional steroids, and found somewhat better outcomes in the 5-FU group (95% vs 50% good or excellent outcomes).

A randomized trial comparing 5-FU + triamcinolone with triamcinolone alone in 120 patients found better results with combination therapy, including better response rates (77% vs 49%, p <0.05) and a lower recurrence rate (17% vs 39%, p <0.05).

A systematic review of 12 RCTs comparing 5-FU + triamcinolone with either drug alone found that the combination was much more effecitve (OR 3.5 to 4.2) and with a lower likelihood of telangectasia (OR 0.24).

A systematic review of 7 RCTs with 461 comparing verapamil with triamcinolone found that the latter resulted in lower height and greater pliability than verapamil, but with more telangectasias and atrophy. A second meta-analysis of 9 RCTs with 567 patients came to the same conclusion regarding efficacy of triamcinolone over verapamil.

A network meta-analysis identified 23 studies with 1513 patients comparing a variety of injected drugs. The order of efficacy was botox-A + corticosteroids > corticosteroids + 5-FU > botox-A > corticosteroids > 5-FU > verapamil.

A pilot study in 37 patients found that those randomized to losartan ointment had better outcomes than those receiving placebo ointment. The mechanism is thought to revolve around angiotensin II's role in fibrosis.

Based on limited quality and low volume evidence, bleomycin may be effective. A systematic review identified 6 studies and concluded based on low quality evidence that bleomycin was more effective than triamcinolone. However, more study is needed.
Dupilumab has uncertain effects on keloids. One case report showed improvement with systemic and intralesional dupilumab, while a systematic review suggested it may cause worsening.
Surgical excision is indicated in keloids older than one year; however, recurrence rates are high.

Certain techniques may reduce recurrences. Avoiding tension by wide undermining and the use of flaps or skin grafts may reduce recurrences. Use of nonreactive sutures, such as monofilament as opposed to braided sutures and early removal of the sutures may reduce inflammation in the wound.
A systematic review identified 20 studies with 926 keloid patients who underwent core excision surgery. Recurrence rates were between 0% and 29%.

Immediate post-excisional radiation therapy (fractionated therapy with a total dose of 10-15 GY) is associated with lower recurrence rates. A systematic review found only one RCT and 11 case series, and no guidance regarding type or dose of radiotherapy.
Cryotherapy may be effective for small lesions, but may cause hypopigmentation.

Silicone gel sheeting: Silicone gel or sheet is placed over the incision as soon as sutures are removed. The silicone is left in place at all times except when cleaning the wound. It is used for up to 6 months after surgery. While thought to be effective, existing trials are of poor quality and the evidence is very low-certainty.

Pressure therapy: Postoperative pressure application effectively reduces recurrence rates. This therapy is mostly utilized to prevent recurrence of earlobe keloids. Compression earrings are available from speciality retailers and are worn 24 hours a day for up to 6 months. Magnetic devices ("Magsil") have also been developed, with silicon gel sheeting on the side contacting the keloid.
A systematic review of 8 studies found that pulsed dye laser may be effective and may be superior to other modalities. A meta-analysis suggested the optimal treatment interval is 5 to 6 weeks.
Fractional ablative lasers CO2 and Er:YAG were recommended based on a second systematic review, primarily of observational studies.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the safety and efficacy of laser therapy in the treatment of hypertrophic and keloid scars.
A network meta-analysis of 18 studies with 550 patients concluded that fractional CO2 laser combined with 5-FU was the most effective laser-based modality.
Recurrences are frequent. B
Growth may stop once keloid reaches a certain size. C
Follow-up for at least 6 months following procedure or trauma. C
Avoid body piercings if there is a previous or family history of keloid formation.
Seek medical advice after lacerations, insect bites and similar injuries if patient has a known tendency to form keloids.
Alert physicians to previous history or family history of keloid formation, especially if undergoing elective medical procedures.
Keloid formation is not common in older patients.
Surgical or medical treatment should be delayed until after pregnancy as there is a high risk of recurrent keloids during pregnancy.
Physical measures such as massage or silicone gel sheeting may be used in the interim.
If possible, surgical treatment of keloid should be delayed until after puberty as there is a high risk of recurrence among children.
Consider medical or surgical treatment of keloids associated with functional impairment.
In children, physical measures to treat keloid should be prioritized over surgical treatments.
